prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and thereby transforming the analysis of exporting, reallocation and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B012 with Melitz and Helpman. The case rests on three things. First, originality: Melitz (2003) is a single, identifiable originating contribution, and Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus FDI, together with his wider new-trade-theory agenda, made it a general research programme. Second, breadth of confirmation: selection into exporting, reallocation across firms and the resulting channel for gains from trade have been tested on firm-level microdata for over twenty years, and the framework now underlies quantitative trade, productivity measurement and macro and growth work on reallocation. Third, attributable credit: two names capture the core mechanism, whereas B022's task-framework credit is diffuse and several other ballots need three-name cuts that leave out major contributors. I treat the 2008 gap in trade prizes only as a timing consideration, not as merit. The chair's question asks what would rank B012 above B022 on common criteria. My answer is that the core insight of B012 has not been revised by later work and its attribution is settled at two names. B022's central magnitudes and persistence are still being revised, and the credit for its theory half lies partly outside the credited set. I do not claim B022 is deficient. Its identification is credible and its question is first-order. This is a judgement about which discovery is more securely established and more cleanly credited, and I hold it with moderate confidence.
statement.case_against: Credit for the heterogeneous-firm agenda is wider than two names. Bernard and Jensen documented the exporter facts, and Eaton and Kortum built a parallel framework. A Melitz-Helpman citation must be worded around the selection and reallocation mechanism so that it does not claim all of that literature. The welfare and gains-from-trade conclusions of the quantitative versions depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity, so the Scientific Background should separate the well-confirmed selection mechanism from the model-dependent welfare magnitudes. Helpman also appears on B007, so naming him here is a choice about which body of his work to honour. Finally, B022 has more explicit round-1 support and answers distributional questions about people and places that trade theory does not address. If the Committee weights societal consequences above conceptual foundation, B022 is the stronger choice, and I would not oppose it.

responses.point: Teorell prefers B022 and treats B012 and B022 as non-competing, since B012 concerns trade theory and quantification and B022 concerns the distributional and labour-market consequences of trade and technology shocks. He says he would not stand in the way of B012 if the Committee wants to recognise trade, and he ranks B022 higher on explanatory reach.
responses.response: I agree the two cover different ground, and that is why I think the Committee cannot choose between them on subject matter. It has to use the common criteria: originality, breadth and durability of confirmation, and attributable credit. On those I still give B012 the edge, because its core mechanism has been stable under two decades of testing and is credited to two names. B022's strongest part, the China-shock evidence, is well identified but its magnitudes and persistence are still being revised, and its task-framework half has originators outside the credited set. Teorell's argument about explanatory reach for people and places is a legitimate weight on social significance. I do not dismiss it, and it is why B022 remains my first alternative. I also welcome his willingness not to block B012, and I would extend the same courtesy to B022.

responses.point: Enflo prefers B022 with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. She says the China-shock attribution is clean and the designs have been replicated and criticised for over a decade. She also concedes that the prize could be read as an empirical-design prize, that magnitudes and persistence are contested, and that task-framework credit is shared with scholars outside the ballot.
responses.response: Her own reservations are close to my reasons for staying with B012. I accept that the China-shock trio is a clean attribution for the trade-shock papers, and I take seriously that a decade of critique is a form of maturity. The difference between us is what the critique shows. Re-analysis of B022 has so far revised the size and duration of its effects, while the selection mechanism in B012 has not been overturned. If the B022 citation is confined to the China-shock and local-labour-market evidence, as she proposes, the credit is defensible. That narrowing would also make B022 a smaller discovery than the broader technology-and-trade framing in some of the other B022 citations. I would want the Scientific Background to address the persistence re-analyses directly, as the chair asks.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B043 (Kiyotaki and Moore) with a clean two-name attribution. He also says that if breadth of confirmed empirical use and trade's absence since 2008 are weighted more heavily, B012 is at least as defensible and he would support it. He ranks B012 second.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour, and I agree B043 is a coherent discovery with unusually clean attribution. My difference is on confirmation. Collateral-driven amplification rests largely on one theoretical paper and its follow-on literature, and direct identification is still debated, as he acknowledges. B012 has had its mechanism checked directly on firm-level data. I would put the 2022 proximity as a lesser concern than that. I do not think the 2008 gap should decide anything, and I agree with Andersson that it is a timing point, not merit. If the Committee believes collateral constraints are a distinct discovery from the 2022 prize and weights conceptual mechanism over breadth of testing, B043 is a respectable choice, which is why it stays among my alternatives.

responses.point: Andersson has moved from B007 to B022 as his lead and keeps B007 as an alternative. He grants that Grossman and Helpman have the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, but that the lobbying model's precise predictions have only mixed empirical support. He also notes that Helpman's overlap with B012 means the Committee must decide which body of his work to honour.
responses.response: His revised view supports my position on Helpman. If the Committee wants to honour Helpman, B012 is the better vehicle on breadth and confirmation, since by Andersson's own account the lobbying model's record is mixed. I would not combine B012 and B007 in one award, since that would credit Helpman twice. I also take his earlier point on Bernard, Jensen and Eaton-Kortum seriously. I do not think it warrants adding a third name, because the ballot does not list them and Redding's extensions build on the core insight. It warrants a citation about firm selection and reallocation as the mechanism, which does not claim the whole literature. If the Committee wanted to include Redding, I would see that as diluting a clean pair, though I could not call it indefensible.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee would treat B012 and B022 as comparable on the common criteria, or whether the choice between them is mainly a judgement about weighting conceptual foundation against societal significance.
How to word a B012 citation so that it recognises the Melitz-Helpman core without understating Bernard-Jensen and Eaton-Kortum, and whether adding Redding would complete or dilute the credit.
How robust the welfare and gains-from-trade conclusions are to functional-form assumptions, as opposed to the well-confirmed selection mechanism.
Whether B022's persistence and magnitude re-analyses will be settled enough to change my ranking, and whether a narrowly worded B022 citation is a smaller or a cleaner discovery than a broad one.
Whether the B043 mechanism is distinct enough from the 2022 prize to move ahead of B012 for members who weight conceptual mechanism over breadth of testing.
My attribution views come from general knowledge and the supplied round-1 files, and I have not independently verified them.
statement.conflict_note: No collaboration with Melitz or Helpman appears in my profile. I disclose that my own research on firm dynamics, creative destruction and misallocation is adjacent to the reallocation themes in B012, and I treat that as expertise, not as merit. I am a long-running co-author of Peter Klenow, a credited name on B026, which is not in my configuration. Per Krusell (secretary) and John Hassler (chair) are frequent co-authors and IIES colleagues. The chair is also a B012 supporter, so his agreement is not independent evidence of merit and I do not count it as such. Friberg's disclosed co-authorship with the chair and Krusell's with me do not bear on any credited name. These connections are disclosed and not adjudicated.
